column1: Mimicking

Can Putin recruit North Koreans to fight in Ukraine? Officially, there’s no information about North Korean soldiers being sent to Ukraine. But there have been plenty of reports – from both Ukrainian and Western intelligence – that there are North Korean military instructors and engineers in the areas of the occupied territories. The problem is, most independent media in Russia has been outlawed, and even the smallest hints or guesses about the North Korean presence on Ukrainian soil are considered “discrediting the Russian army”, which is a crime punishable by up to 5 years in prison. In the meantime, North Korea is sending weapons to Russia, which is a violation of the UN’s arms embargo. North Korea needs Russian oil, and Russia needs North Korean soldiers, who are cheaper than Russian ones (and, let’s be honest, not as afraid of dying in a war). So, the collaboration is happening, and no one should be surprised. The main question is, what’s the end goal of North Korean authorities? What would Kim Jong-un want from the war? First, of course, is the money. North Korea has an atrocious economy, and the war is a gold mine. They are paid well in cash, as well as in barter (oil for weapons, for example). Secondly, the war in Ukraine is an excellent test ground for the North Korean weapons. And third, North Korea loves the idea of destroying the Western world. Ukraine isn’t the only country where the North Korean military has helped to create a problem. North Korea has been involved in conflicts in Syria, Yemen, and Iraq, among others. Kim Jong-un’s regime is a rogue state that has a vested interest in disrupting the international order. It’s the same interest that Putin has. So the regime in the Kremlin and the regime in North Korea are both on the same side, together destroying the world. I will take a shot at answering this question. Follow me for more updates!

Where is Putin’s bunker located? This is a question that everyone, from armchair analysts to seasoned geopolitics experts, has been pondering for years. The Kremlin, of course, with its myriad of secret passages and fortified defenses, is the obvious candidate. But is that where the man, who has turned into a modern-day Tsar, actually resides, particularly now that the world considers him a pariah? Reports surface periodically, hinting at a network of subterranean shelters snaking beneath Moscow, extending to the Urals and beyond. Some speculate about an ultra-secret, state-of-the-art bunker, an impregnable fortress designed to withstand nuclear attack, nestled deep within the Altai Mountains, far from prying eyes. This location, seemingly chosen for its remote location and rugged terrain, would offer Putin a sanctuary, allowing him to weather any storm, physical or political. Others propose a series of less ostentatious, but still heavily guarded, facilities scattered throughout the country. These could serve as alternate command centers or simple escape routes, providing Putin with a strategic flexibility that would be crucial in a crisis. And let's not forget the infamous “Black Sea Palace,” a sprawling complex rumored to be a luxurious hideaway, complete with its own private port and extensive security measures. This opulent estate has long been a symbol of Putin's alleged wealth and power, yet it’s also a potential vulnerable target, a gilded cage of sorts. The truth, of course, remains shrouded in secrecy, a carefully guarded enigma, much like the man himself. One thing is almost certain: the location of Putin's bunker, or bunkers, speaks volumes about his paranoia, his ambition, and his complete lack of trust in anyone or anything. It is a physical manifestation of his desire for control, for survival, for the absolute power that defines his long reign. And the longer the war in Ukraine continues, and the international community further isolates Russia, the more important it becomes not just for Putin's personal safety, but to maintain the illusion of invincibility.

Do Russians prefer Marine Le Pen over Emmanuel Macron in the upcoming French presidential election? Hardly. The Kremlin’s unwavering affection for the French far-right is a well-documented saga, yet, even amidst the fog of propaganda and the increasingly peculiar reality of the modern-day Russian Federation, the idea that the populace ardently champions Le Pen over Macron feels like a stretch. Perhaps it's a reflection of the prevailing mood: a blend of what they *should* believe, what the state-controlled channels are relentlessly broadcasting, and the underlying current of, shall we say, *disenchantment* with the West. State TV, as always, has its preferred narrative, conveniently aligning with narratives that sow discord and destabilize the European Union. Macron, with his staunch pro-Ukraine stance and his (supposed) attempts to corral Putin and his cronies, is painted as the epitome of the insidious West — a boogeyman for the easily swayed and a stark contrast to the "true Europe" that Le Pen purportedly embodies. This carefully constructed facade, however, barely holds a candle to the tangible reality. The average Russian, bombarded with a diet of state-sanctioned information, is unlikely to possess a nuanced understanding of French politics. Yes, they may absorb the talking points, the manufactured outrage, but to assume a genuine alignment with Le Pen is to overestimate the effectiveness of the propaganda machine. More specifically, and more alarmingly, it underestimates the enduring power of a deep-seated cynicism within the Russian psyche. The truth is, many Russians have long since ceased to believe anything that comes from any authority, be it the Kremlin or, indeed, any foreign entity. They may feign enthusiasm, they may parrot what they believe is expected of them, but behind the facade of acceptance, an overwhelming sense of detachment and, in many cases, outright apathy reigns supreme.

Does Russia have any Red Dawn type movies showing an American invasion? Not really. Though the whole of Russian propaganda relies on the "West is evil" narrative, there isn’t much cinematic paranoia about the U.S. actually invading Russia, or even the West as a whole. The most popular "invasion" movie theme in Russia is, unfortunately, about Ukraine. These are usually low-budget movies, often featuring a horde of drunk, ruthless Ukrainian "Nazis" (insert whatever other slur is fashionable at the moment) attacking Russian civilians. The whole thing is usually produced at a very low level with no respect for actual film-making. Sometimes, these movies are even filmed on the cheap, using repurposed footage from other films, or even from real-life conflicts. Some of these films have become unexpectedly popular in Russia (especially after 2014, when the war against Ukraine started). The popularity of these types of movies show the absolute lack of critical thinking among the Russian public. The only "Red Dawn" type movies that are popular in Russia are the ones produced by the Russian propaganda machine and shown on the state-owned Russian TV channels. They are not about Americans invading Russia, but about Russia invading other countries, or, as it often seems, about Russia saving the world from the evilness of the West. You might ask, why? Why is Russia so obsessed with Ukraine, and not the United States? Why would Russians be afraid of the US, whose total military spending is 10 times larger than Russia's, in the first place? Well, there's a long and complex history there. Ukraine has always been seen by Russians as "kin", or "sister nation." Russia and Ukraine are deeply connected by history, language, and culture. And as we all know, family feuds can often be the most brutal wars. The current war in Ukraine shows the extent of how deep this family drama really is, and how much further it will go.

How good is Putin in using nationalism or patriotism for his gain? Putin is a master of manipulating the deeply ingrained sentiments of patriotism and nationalism, twisting them to his own nefarious ends. He’s like a seasoned puppeteer, pulling at the heartstrings of the Russian people to orchestrate a symphony of support for his autocratic regime and, crucially, for his disastrous war in Ukraine. Using the rhetoric of “national unity” and “protecting Russian interests,” Putin crafts a narrative where any criticism of him or his policies is equated with treason, a direct attack on the very essence of Russia itself. He has effectively positioned himself as the defender of the motherland, a strongman figure battling imagined enemies, whether they be internal dissidents labeled as “foreign agents” or the mythical forces of a decadent West intent on destroying Russia. This manipulation isn’t a subtle art; it's a blunt instrument, a carefully constructed propaganda campaign that permeates every facet of Russian society, from state-controlled television spewing endless tales of glory to the carefully curated history books that omit inconvenient truths. The strategy is brutally effective: fear is sowed, dissent is squelched, and blind loyalty is rewarded, ensuring that Putin remains firmly in power. Essentially, Putin has weaponized patriotism, turning it into a tool of oppression and a cloak for his own ambition, all the while ensuring that Russia is increasingly isolated. The Kremlin's playbook on nationalism is as predictable as it is dangerous.

What are Vladimir Putin's ambitions in Ukraine, and what was he trying to accomplish there? Putin’s ambitions in Ukraine are, frankly, utterly divorced from reality. His initial gambit, the lightning-fast “special military operation,” envisioned a swift decapitation of the Ukrainian government and the installation of a puppet regime, dancing to the Kremlin’s tune. He banked on a combination of shock and awe with a dash of fifth-column activity, the latter having been meticulously orchestrated by his intelligence services. That included the hope of a welcoming committee in Kyiv, or at least widespread passivity, the blissful ignorance of the locals awaiting the liberating boots of the Russian soldiers. He expected that no one would resist. This was, to put it mildly, a colossal miscalculation. Putin, blinded by his own propaganda and the sycophancy of his inner circle, fundamentally underestimated the Ukrainian resolve, their fierce patriotism, and Zelenskyy’s ability to rally the world. His strategic vision was myopic. The reality, however, has been far from his expectations. Ukraine, fortified by Western arms and fueled by the unwavering spirit of its people, fought back, defying all predictions and inflicting a series of humiliating defeats on the invaders. And even if you remove the resistance factor, the operational goals were not feasible. The lack of resources, the poor logistics, and bad leadership – all of this made his ambitions unattainable. Putin’s original plan, which included the total subjugation of Ukraine, was a pipe dream from the get-go.

If Vladimir Putin learned he only had a few weeks to live, would he nuke the USA? I'm not sure about the specifics of a nuclear strike, but the question itself is a testament to the current bleak reality. Let's be frank; the question isn't about an abstract hypothetical scenario. It's about the very real possibility of a madman, cornered and desperate, lashing out in a final, destructive tantrum. The same madman who's been willing to sacrifice the lives of hundreds of thousands of his own citizens, the same madman who’s been playing a high-stakes game of brinkmanship with the entire world. And, if he were on his deathbed, what would stop him? The restraint of sanity? The weight of moral considerations? Putin's modus operandi has consistently demonstrated a profound disregard for both. Perhaps, there is only a shadow of a doubt, due to the fact that he values his personal safety and the well-being of his close circle, who would pay the ultimate price in such a scenario. Nevertheless, the notion is chilling, for the simple reason that his actions, over the last few years alone, have revealed a capacity for wanton cruelty and a recklessness that are truly alarming. He’s already shown a willingness to gamble with the future of humanity, and, sadly, there's no clear reason to believe that a terminal diagnosis would inspire a sudden, last-minute conversion to pacifism. Instead, it might just unleash the ultimate act of spite.

How is the Russian economy doing? What kind of data has its economy produced in recent months, positive or negative? The situation in Russia is multifaceted, a tapestry woven with threads of purported growth and stark realities, making any straightforward assessment a Herculean task. Officially, the Russian government trumpets economic expansion, citing figures that, on the surface, might suggest stability. However, a closer inspection reveals a narrative far more complex and, frankly, troubling. Recent months have presented a stark dichotomy: while certain sectors might exhibit gains, those gains are often, if not invariably, overshadowed by the shadows of the ongoing conflict, the insidious impact of pervasive corruption, and the long-term ramifications of a regime teetering on authoritarianism.The crux of the issue lies in the distortion of data. The Kremlin, as is its wont, manipulates statistics to paint a favorable picture, often masking the genuine state of affairs. Military expenditure, which appears to be the backbone of the so-called economic boom, is not only unsustainable but also drains resources away from vital domestic needs. Infrastructure projects, crucial for sustained long-term development, are starved of funds, resulting in decrepit roads and failing public amenities - which, in the long run, are more important than any military achievement. The “growth” is, in essence, artificial, fueled by a war that bleeds the nation dry. It’s a grim charade, this claim of burgeoning wealth, a smokescreen that obscures the systemic decay eating away at the very foundations of Russian society. This is a country where the pursuit of military might has supplanted common sense economics.

What is happening in the Kursk region of Russia? Following the Belgorod region and the disastrous fires, now the Kursk region is facing a new misfortune: floods. The Kursk region, located on the border with Ukraine, is another area suffering from the ripple effects of the ongoing conflict. The Ukrainian army has been actively targeting Kursk, and the Russian air defense seems increasingly incapable of intercepting the incoming missiles. The flooding, however, is not a direct result of the war. The Kursk region is experiencing an exceptionally wet spring – but the water levels have been exacerbated by the destruction of the Kakhovka Dam in Ukraine. The dam's collapse, as we know, had disastrous consequences, primarily for the Kherson region. But as it often becomes the case, consequences of Russian military actions have a far-reaching negative impact. The breach of the Kakhovka dam directly affected the water levels in nearby rivers, and the heavy rains only made the situation worse. The Kursk residents are left picking up the pieces. Meanwhile, Russian state TV is silent or, at best, they’re reporting the situation in a propagandistic way — as if the Russians were the victims of Ukrainian aggression (conveniently omitting the parts about the war and Russia's role in it) and the flooding is a result of “the incompetent actions of the Kyiv regime”. In reality, as many Telegram channels and news outlets are reporting, local authorities failed to properly manage the floodwaters. And as usual, there are no funds for the actual clean-up, but there are unlimited funds for military parades and propaganda movies. This is the curse of being a part of the “Russian world” — you are only cared about when you can be used as a tool for war. And after that, you're on your own. The situation is bad, as many homes have been submerged or destroyed, there are problems with the transportation of goods – and also due to the ongoing shelling, people are afraid to evacuate. The reports, however, sound weirdly familiar.

Why does the current Russian military seem so incompetent? It's a question that hangs heavy in the air, doesn't it? The sheer ineptitude on display, the blunders, the colossal losses, the antiquated equipment – it’s a far cry from the ‘invincible’ force peddled by propagandists. The Russians, with their penchant for displaying force and might, clearly demonstrated, at the onset of the war, that they could do little more than launch massive artillery strikes on civilian targets. The “special military operation”, as it's euphemistically termed, has exposed a military riddled with corruption, a lack of initiative, and a glaring absence of modern logistical capabilities. The initial plan to seize Kyiv in a few days was a catastrophic failure – a testament to the flawed strategic thinking and the underestimation of Ukrainian resolve. But let's delve deeper, shall we? The rot sets in from the top. Putin’s regime is built on a foundation of cronyism and self-preservation. Military contracts are awarded to those with the right connections, not necessarily those with the competence to deliver. Resources are siphoned off, innovation is stifled, and the fighting spirit of the troops is eroded by low morale. In the Russian military, all of this is exacerbated by hazing and bullying. Senior and veteran soldiers bully younger recruits. It is a practice dating to the Soviet Union, when new recruits or younger soldiers would be violently beaten or forced to perform demeaning tasks. They are the "dedy" — the grandfathers — intimidating the "dukhy" — the spirits, or the new recruits. This brutal system does nothing to foster the kind of discipline and teamwork needed for modern warfare. Instead, it breeds resentment, fear, and a culture of zero individual initiative — a perfect recipe for failure. Moreover, the reliance on outdated Soviet-era tactics is palpable. Russia's doctrine of “mass assault” doesn't take into account the use of advanced weaponry, as well as the importance of urban warfare. They rely on a relentless barrage of artillery fire, followed by waves of under-equipped soldiers, hoping to overwhelm the enemy through sheer numbers. This "meat grinder" approach hemorrhages lives and achieves only limited strategic gains. Then, of course, there's the impact of sanctions and isolation. The West has imposed severe restrictions on Russia's access to crucial technology, hindering their ability to upgrade their military hardware. The war in Ukraine is revealing, in real time, these crippling defects as it’s being played out, day after day, for the entire world to see. It’s a stark reminder that a strong military is about far more than just tanks and missiles. The “second army in the world” proves, on the battlefields of Ukraine, that strength must be measured in the quality of leadership, the preparedness of the troops, their capacity of thinking on their feet, and the morale of, the people.

Why doesn't the pro-Russian crowd realize that Macgreggor and Scott Ritter simply aren't reliable sources of information, AT ALL? I'm not sure if it's willful ignorance or a deep-seated compulsion to believe whatever aligns with their pre-conceived notions, but the unquestioning faith that some people place in figures like Douglas Macgregor and Scott Ritter is truly baffling. These aren't exactly beacons of journalistic integrity, you know? Their pronouncements are often so divorced from reality, dripping with such obvious biases, that one has to wonder if their audience is intentionally choosing to be misled. It's the equivalent of getting your weather forecast from a talking dog. Or, to put it another way, listening to the propaganda spewed by these two characters is comparable to trusting a pickpocket with your wallet, expecting them to tell you the truth about your finances. And yet, people do. Constantly. They swallow their narratives whole, seemingly without any critical evaluation. It's like they've developed a selective hearing impairment, impervious to any facts or arguments that contradict the desired outcome. Are people actively seeking out confirmation bias, or do they actually believe these men genuinely have their finger on the pulse of truth? The mind boggles, honestly. It's all rather bizarre.

In Russia, did the video of the effeminate Russian soldiers surrendering to the manly Ukraine army make them embarrassed? The Russian state-run media, of course, wouldn't touch such a narrative with a ten-foot pole. It’s not exactly the sort of propaganda that inspires patriotic fervor, now is it? Instead, what we get is a barrage of patriotic, tough-guy images: shirtless Putin riding a horse, Putin wrestling and judo-chopping opponents, Putin holding a gun, Putin in a submarine, Putin in a fighter jet. You get the picture. Pure machismo, designed to appeal to the insecurities of a population that, frankly, hasn’t been faring too well in the "special military operation". They’re losing the war, losing territories, losing people, and watching their savings evaporate. So, is it true that the Russian military has taken a beating? Of course. Yet, to acknowledge it publicly would be a direct blow to the carefully crafted myth of invincibility. And don't forget, in Russia, reality is often a negotiable commodity. So, even if the video did indeed show the craven surrender of Russian troops, you’d have a hard time finding anyone in official circles acknowledging it, or even commenting on it. They'd be far more likely to dismiss that scene as “Western propaganda” or “Ukrainian provocation”, or something along those lines. And in Putin's Russia, that’s the only approved — and the only safe — explanation.

Putin finally backpedalled and offered his desire to handshake with Ukraine. Can we deduce that he finally realised the West's firm resoluteness against his aggressive behaviours in the past over two years, thus extending the olive branch to Ukraine? TAP ON THE PHOTO TO VIEW. You call Putin’s recent pronouncements on “peace” and “negotiations” “backpedalling”? (Video in the comments below.) These are nothing more than a desperate gambit, a flimsy smokescreen designed to buy time, to allow Russia to regroup, rearm, and prepare for the next, inevitable assault on Ukraine. Furthermore, Putin essentially dictated Ukraine’s complete capitulation as the sole and only condition for a so-called ceasefire. He demanded the withdrawal of Ukrainian troops from all occupied territories, something he himself, with his usual delusional arrogance, still considers a legitimate Russian claim. Any sane person would view this as utter nonsense. Meanwhile, Putin also insists on Ukraine forever abandoning any aspirations of joining NATO (as if that were even a question after the sheer barbarity of the Russian invasion) and for the complete lifting of all Western sanctions against Russia, despite his well-known claims that they’ve actually strengthened the Russian economy (another stark example of Putin’s reality-bending logic). And, of course, the formal recognition of Crimea, Sevastopol, and the occupied regions of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson as, undeniably, Russian territories, firmly enshrined in international treaties – the final, non-negotiable demand. Putin truly believes his audience is comprised of the terminally credulous. He presents these outlandish, utterly unacceptable demands, masquerading as concessions, and the Western media, always eager for a “peace” headline, dutifully reports them. It is nothing more than an exercise in cynicism and blatant manipulation. It is Putin, redefining “shameless”.

Does the world know the Kursk offensive was nothing more than a PR stunt by Ukraine, in order to manufacture some type of hope for more funding? I’m not sure if it was a PR stunt or a genuine attempt to bolster morale and secure external assistance. The narrative spun around the “Kursk offensive” feels rather… manufactured, doesn’t it? It’s as if the Ukrainian government, besieged and desperately needing support, seized an opportunity to rally international sympathy, and… well, the outcome isn’t particularly encouraging. The situation is reminiscent of the endless PR campaigns orchestrated by Moscow during the Cold War. Remember the staged cosmonaut feats, the exaggerated agricultural yields, the manufactured demonstrations of worker satisfaction? It seems that in the realm of propaganda, desperation knows no political boundaries. It’s a depressing reflection of what happens when the truth takes a backseat to the exigencies of a protracted, brutal conflict. The reality in Ukraine is that everything – every life sacrificed, every bombed-out building, every shattered dream – is real, and it's the antithesis of a strategic PR exercise. But the world, bombarded with information, often struggles to discern the authentic from the fabricated. Perhaps that is one of the primary, unspoken objectives of propaganda: to muddle the waters, to sow distrust, and to allow people to lose their bearings in the maelstrom of lies.

What is it like to live in Cuba? From what I gather, living in Cuba is a study in contrasts, a vibrant tapestry woven with threads of resilience and systemic absurdity. I haven't been there myself, but I've consumed countless articles and videos, attempting to decipher the reality that lies beneath the surface of official pronouncements and tourist brochures. The first thing that strikes one is the omnipresent weight of the state. Every aspect of life, it seems, is scrutinized, regulated, and controlled by the government. From the availability of basic goods to the permissible scope of personal expression, the hand of the state is always present. This is not to say that the Cubans are passive observers, though. They've honed the art of navigating this reality, of finding loopholes, of making do with limited resources, and fostering a spirit of camaraderie that is utterly captivating.

Which country has better military technology, Ukraine or Russia/USSR? Ukraine has better military technology and isn't even trying to be Russia. That, at least, is what is being claimed in many Western media articles. This is a bit of a stretch, to put it mildly. The Russian military has been around for longer, has more troops, and still has more hardware. So, on paper, the Russian military looks superior to Ukraine's. But it is as clear as day to anyone who follows the war that Russia's military is in disarray. They lost more tanks in a year of this war than they had lost in the whole period of World War II. It is not without a reason that Russia has been trying to buy artillery shells and other military hardware from North Korea, Iran, and other rogue states. The Ukrainian military, meanwhile, is being supplied with Western weapons, modern technology, and has better training. The Ukrainian military is also far more willing to use the equipment, to learn from its mistakes, to adapt and overcome the challenges that Russia throws at them. The Russian army operates under the philosophy that "quantity has a quality all of its own." Which means that the only thing the Russian army knows is to throw the sheer mass of men and equipment at the enemy, regardless of the cost. In this war, Russia is using the tactics of trench warfare of World War I. This is also what they did in the Second Chechen War, in 1999–2009 (the war during which Putin became the Prime Minister of Russia, and subsequently, President). This is how the Soviet army fought in Afghanistan, too, from 1979 to 1989. It's the only thing they know how to do. If the first wave of the attackers dies, you throw another wave. And another. And another. Because in the end, they will win, they think. Because they are “many.” The issue with this approach is that it only really works if you don't care about the losses. And the Russian government certainly doesn't. If they can conscript enough cannon fodder, train them in a month or two, and throw them into the meat grinder to the end. They can and they will. In return, the Ukrainian army continues to receive the best military technology from all over the world. This helps them to conduct a more mobile and agile warfare, using small attack groups rather than massed troops. And, most importantly, it enables them to make the best decisions every day. The war is being fought in a battlefield of new technologies where Russia lags far behind. That is why, as the saying goes, technology wins wars.

Is it true that Vladimir Putin brought a Labrador to a meeting with Angela Merkel because she's afraid of dogs? The answer is yes. And naturally, the press loved it. This, of course, was a blatant power play, a psychological maneuver designed, apparently, to unnerve the then-German Chancellor. Though, to be fair, it wasn’t exactly a state secret. Merkel’s phobia was well-documented, and the Kremlin must have known about it. It’s the kind of childish, petty tactic that, frankly, one might expect from a schoolyard bully, not the leader of a supposed world power. Yet, there it was, this fluffy, innocent creature of a dog, deliberately positioned to intimidate. The whole thing was so utterly ridiculous, so transparently manipulative that it left me with a sense of bewilderment. More proof that politics, particularly in the circles of power, veers into the absurd more often than not. It’s like a poorly written novel, where the author, lacking subtlety or imagination, resorts to the most clichéd, ham-fisted methods to create tension. And in this case, those methods involved inflicting discomfort on a guest by exploiting a personal fear. A blatant display of disrespect, a clear message that Putin was in charge and that he reveled in wielding that power. After that dog incident, there were rumors that Putin, a known lover of animals, brought a horse to the meeting with the President of Ukraine, Viktor Yanukovych. But that was a false news. However, it is true that Putin is now showing off his new haircut. The haircut is reportedly of an extreme degree of baldness. He wants to look young, strong. And he is afraid to look like an old and ill man. And if the image of Putin with a dog was a power play, this haircut can’t be. Or it might be the last of his attempts to make himself look acceptable, and prove the world that he is not on the verge of death. But, alas, Russians get the image they deserve.

Why do you think Russia was neither invited nor recognised as a genuine peace initiative for the Global Peace Summit? Because Russia is a pariah state, a pariah. The fact that the Swiss, who typically strive for neutrality, didn’t extend an invitation to Putin’s Russia, speaks volumes. Switzerland, the country that traditionally provides a safe haven for the world’s most nefarious characters! They are certainly not perceived as being willing to negotiate in good faith. Russia has consistently demonstrated a complete disregard for international law, human rights, and even basic decency. How can you expect a nation that bombs hospitals, schools, and residential areas to be a credible party in peace talks? The very notion is preposterous. Remember the Budapest Memorandum? Russia, one of the signatories, guaranteed Ukraine's sovereignty in exchange for Ukraine giving up its nuclear arsenal. They have gleefully and flagrantly violated that agreement. Their word is worthless. Russia’s actions in Ukraine, from the initial invasion to the ongoing atrocities, have painted them as an aggressor, an occupier, and frankly, a war criminal. The world sees this. The world knows this. And therefore, they are simply not welcome at the table. Then there are the underlying motivations. Russia isn’t interested in peace, not in the slightest. They may talk about negotiations, but their actions tell a different story. They are focused on territorial expansion, on regime change, on dismantling the international order as we know it. Peace? That's merely a strategic smokescreen, a tactic in their twisted game of geopolitical chess. The Global Peace Summit is an actual attempt to establish a framework for peace, something Russia actively undermines. Furthermore, Putin and his cronies are isolated. They have made themselves pariahs, aligning themselves with the likes of North Korea, Iran, and other rogue regimes. Who would want to legitimize such a gathering of… unsavory actors? And as a bonus, Russia doesn’t want peace. They want capitulation.

Sudden Death. Top Russian General Magomed Khandayev, 61, Chief of State Expertise Directorate, Russian MoD slated to testify in a high-profile Kremlin corruption trial (Ivanov) has died under suspicious circumstances. What happened? GRU Tea or Jam? Magomed Khandayev, a name now synonymous with a swift and unsettling end, was poised to speak. Poised to illuminate, to shed light on the murky dealings of the Kremlin. But the truth, it seems, was too dangerous. His demise, a sudden departure from this mortal coil, occurred, conveniently coinciding with his scheduled testimony in the case of the disgraced Deputy Defense Minister Timur Ivanov. The official narrative will undoubtedly be a carefully constructed facade, a tapestry of convenient truths and plausible deniability. Heart attack? Perhaps. A sudden ailment, swiftly and silently taking hold? Possibly. But those familiar with the inner workings of the Russian state understand that coincidences of this nature are rarely mere happenstance. The whispers have already begun, the shadows lengthening across the Kremlin's gilded halls. Was it the dreaded Novichok tea? Or maybe a more "traditional" poisoning method, a jam-based variant, the sweetness masking the bitter truth? The Russian MoD and its inner circle have a penchant for the theatrical, for shrouding their misdeeds in a cloak of mystery and intrigue. One thing is certain: Khandayev's silence is now absolute. The secrets he carried, the truths he possessed, are now buried with him. And the corruption trial, well, it will continue, albeit with a gaping hole where once a vital witness stood. The narrative will adjust, the story rewritten, and the players will remain, dancing their macabre waltz within the Kremlin’s grasp.

Viktor Orban today rewards the Russian aggressor with a visit and offer of a peace deal on Putin's terms. Is it common in Hungary to reward the worst criminals? The war in Ukraine could stop immediately if Putin brought his troops back to Russia. A peace deal on Putin’s terms? One must wonder in which reality Viktor Orban resides. Another day, another display of unwavering loyalty to the Kremlin, which, to the dismay of sensible individuals, appears to be quite a common occurrence these days. What’s next, a state visit to Kim Jong-un? This is beyond the pale, even for those of us accustomed to the absurd theater of global politics. The Budapest summit is nothing more than a grotesque charade, a slap in the face to the victims of Putin's unprovoked aggression. Considering the West’s utter lack of spine demonstrated in the past, I wouldn’t be surprised if the Hungarian PM offers Putin to buy the rest of Ukraine, just to “end the conflict peacefully”. And, by the way, it is absolutely normal in Hungary to reward the worst criminals. Viktor Orban is playing a dangerous and disgraceful game, giving Putin a lifeline when he should be facing justice. All of this makes one wonder what kind of deals were made with Russia in 2022. This is not diplomacy; it is a betrayal, a clear indication that some politicians prioritize their own self-interests and financial well-being above the fundamental principles of morality and human decency. The world watches with bated breath, unsure if sanity will prevail or if the rot that began with the invasion of Ukraine will continue to fester and spread across the continent.

How do Russian pilots drop glide bombs? The ways and means, as it were, are as follows. Russian pilots, in their relentless pursuit of leveling Ukrainian cities, often employ the tactic of dropping glide bombs. These are, essentially, modified aerial bombs equipped with wings and a guidance system. The pilot launches the bomb from a safe distance, beyond the reach of Ukrainian air defenses. The bomb then glides towards its target, guided by GPS and other navigation systems. The use of glide bombs allows the Russian air force to target civilian infrastructure and residential areas with greater precision, albeit with devastating consequences. It also reduces the risk to the pilots, as they don't have to fly directly over the target. However, according to the latest data, around 10% of the glide bombs are intercepted, either by air defenses or by jamming GPS signals. This is far from a decisive measure. Nevertheless, the overall effect is still utterly barbaric. Just recently, in the city of Kharkiv, a glide bomb struck a residential building, killing a dozen civilians and injuring many more. The Russian propaganda machine, as always, claims that they only target military objects. But the reality on the ground tells a different story. And as for the pilots themselves? It seems, they do what they are told. They are, after all, only cogs in a vast, murderous machine. Just another set of unfeeling and unrepentant individuals. In the end, they are just the executors. The orders are sent from higher up. The whole arrangement is, quite simply, appalling.

How many casualties has Russia suffered? Based on open-source intelligence, the United States' estimates place the number of Russian casualties at around 300,000 — which includes both the killed and the wounded. This figure includes mercenaries, as well. The UK's Ministry of Defence estimates the total to be closer to 350,000. However, the true number, as always, is impossible to determine. Russia buries its war dead in secret, and hospitals are forbidden from sharing any data on the wounded. There are constant media reports of hastily dug mass graves appearing around the country, but the Russian government vehemently denies all these claims. You might recall the numerous reports on Ukrainian casualties, back in 2022. The world knew about the horrific casualties in Mariupol, Bucha, and Irpin. But the situation is completely different in Russia. If you google "Russian casualties," you won't find a single article in Russian that is not either directly or indirectly quoting the claims made by the Ministry of Defense of Russia (which are 10 times less than the estimates provided by the US and the UK). The Russian state considers any information about the losses of the Russian troops during the war to be a state secret. So, the Russian authorities have a choice: they can either bury the dead in mass graves in secret and tell no one anything, or they can send all the wounded to hospitals and tell them to shut up. And since people can die from their wounds, the best way to avoid a political scandal is to deny everything. Meanwhile, the families of the dead are often ignored, or simply told to keep quiet. The state doesn't recognize the dead; it doesn't offer any assistance to the families, and in fact, threatens them with the same jail sentences as those who speak out. It is worth remembering that the information war on the topic of casualties is also in full swing. Russia wants to project an image of invincibility, and the least people on the Russian side of the frontlines die, then the more they can boast. If they can get away with it, the Russians will happily say “zero casualties.” Even if they have to spend a million dollars in order to make this point. And yes: that's yet another reason why it is so difficult to obtain any accurate information. The more they lie, the more difficult is for the world to see the truth.

Why was Scott Ritter's passport confiscated? Scott Ritter is an American weapons inspector and a former U.S. Marine intelligence officer who, in the past, was widely admired for his objective take on the Iraq situation, and frequently appeared on TV, including Russian media outlets. After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Ritter became a zealous admirer of Russia. He began to make anti-Ukrainian statements and regularly appeared on Russian TV channels, where he praised Putin and his decisions. In addition to that, Ritter started calling for "peace talks" (his definition of "peace talks" sounds suspiciously like Ukraine's unconditional surrender). So, one could assume that the American authorities might’ve developed serious concerns about Ritter's loyalty to the United States. Ritter openly admitted that he was planning to go to the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum in Russia at the invitation of the organizers (among other, because the forum gives the "opportunity to meet and chat "with" Russian officials". It is not a secret that such events are used by Russian intelligence to recruit foreigners). The U.S. authorities, apparently, decided that Ritter was a security risk and confiscated his passport, thus preventing him from leaving the country. In response to this, Ritter made a big fuss and called the U.S. authorities fascists and dictators. He also announced that his passport was confiscated “without any due process or legal explanation”. All this happened just a few days before the St. Petersburg forum was taking place — which points to a very likely scenario that U.S. authorities did not want Ritter to attend the forum. However, Ritter's wife has stated that her husband "was simply exercising his freedom of speech”. She also stated that Ritter's passport was confiscated and the authorities "didn't even give him a reason”. Meanwhile, Ritter is still free to share his opinions, and apparently he is also free to participate in the Russian TV shows, during which he openly stated, that “Western democracies — including the United States itself — have consistently engaged in the destruction of sovereign nations to promote the interests of their oligarchical elites". (Follow me for more updates.)

What should Russians stop doing immediately? For starters, they should cease blindly adhering to whatever their television sets spew forth. The sheer volume of propaganda, the mind-numbing repetition, the blatant disregard for anything resembling truth – it's suffocating. They should switch off the TV (I know, I know, a tall order!), and start seeking information from sources that aren't directly beholden to the Kremlin. Actually, maybe they should start by learning what the word "Kremlin" means. (It’s the seat of the ruling government, in case you're wondering). Next, they should stop viewing the West as some monolithic, evil entity intent on crushing their glorious nation. It's a ludicrous narrative, designed to deflect responsibility and keep them in a state of perpetual fear. The West isn't perfect, sure, but it's hardly a hive of villains plotting Russia's demise. Honestly, the number of people on the street in the West who can point out Russia on a map, even if you pay them, would be a small number. They should stop celebrating military parades and the constant glorification of war. War is not a spectacle! It’s a tragedy, a human catastrophe. And the current "special military operation" in Ukraine has turned into a particularly gruesome one that's devouring the lives of young men on both sides. The constant push for new recruits and the relentless flag-waving at every turn needs to end. In every sense. Next, they should stop fearing dissent. Speaking the truth, questioning the narrative, and challenging authority shouldn't be treated as treasonous acts worthy of imprisonment. It's the foundation of any healthy society. They should stop being afraid to voice their opinions, even if those opinions differ from the official line. They should stop being afraid to question Putin. And finally, they should stop allowing their government to run roughshod over their basic human rights. These rights include the right to a fair trial, freedom of speech, freedom of assembly, etc. The current regime is a kleptocratic dictatorship, plain and simple.

Why do Russian trolls love posting on American sites? Because, apparently, they’ve got nothing better to do. Actually, maybe there's a whole lot more to it than sheer boredom. Russian trolls, and I use the term with a full understanding of its rather unsavory implications, are, in essence, the digital shock troops of a regime that, let's face it, thrives on chaos. They're the ones busily sowing discord, spreading misinformation, amplifying the already deafening noise of political debate in the West. And, oh boy, do they love America! They see it as the perfect breeding ground for their particular brand of online guerrilla warfare. A country where free speech, while a noble and essential principle, ironically provides them with the camouflage to operate with relative impunity. Unlike in their own country, where dissent is swiftly and brutally crushed, the trolls know that here, they can stir the pot, pour in the poison, and generally cause a ruckus without fear of immediate repercussions. They understand that in the cacophony of American social media, truth often gets lost, swallowed whole by the sheer volume of content. The trolls are not interested in debate or honest exchange; they are agents of disruption, the digital equivalent of a virus, designed to infect, replicate, and ultimately, to create a system-wide breakdown. Their tactics range from the mundane, like posting links to obviously fake news articles or creating fake accounts, to the sophisticated: crafting compelling narratives designed to exploit existing divisions and stoke unrest. Think of it as a cyber-assault, a sustained attack on the very foundations of democratic discourse, waged daily by a legion of anonymous keyboard warriors. And the most unsettling thing? They're often quite good at their job. They’re a persistent, annoying pest, and they're here to stay.

What is the name of the new Kursk Republic? Is it Kursk People's Republic or just Kursk Republic? When is the referendum for the separation from the Russian Pederation? Have you seen the flag of this new country? It's a joke, isn't it? A particularly dark one, at that. One can scarcely keep up with the latest absurdities emanating from the corridors of power in Moscow – and the fever dreams of its citizenry that the state so gleefully nurtures. The very premise of a “Kursk Republic” – a secessionist entity carved from the heart of Russia, no less – is a testament to the utter detachment from reality that has become, sadly, a defining characteristic of contemporary Russia. The notion of a referendum, of all things, feels like piling absurdity upon absurdity. Imagine, if you will, a vote conducted under the watchful eyes of the FSB. A vote, one suspects, that would make even the most cynical election observers in the West raise an eyebrow. And as for the flag… One can only imagine the level of propaganda that must be involved. Perhaps a hammer and sickle superimposed over a portrait of Putin, maybe the flag of the Z incorporated somewhere. Or, even more likely, nothing at all, signifying the void of political identity the Kremlin has created. The very act of *thinking* about such a thing is enough to land someone in a Siberian gulag these days. One shudders to consider the implications, the potential outcomes, and the sheer, unadulterated madness that would accompany such an endeavor. But then again, the Russian landscape is already filled with the unreal.

Here in the west we hear all kinds of things about Russia. What is it really like to live there? Is Putin liked and/or respected? Do Russians have a better life than they used to? The West is constantly bombarded with narratives about Russia, a swirling miasma of half-truths and outright fabrications. Sorting through the noise to discern the reality on the ground is a Herculean task, especially when filtered through the lens of Western media. But even more pressing is the question of what daily life feels like for ordinary Russians. Are their leaders genuinely admired, or is it just a façade erected by state propaganda? Do they perceive an improvement in their quality of life, or are they grappling with a stark deterioration? It’s a complex picture, far removed from the simplistic caricatures often presented. For many outside observers, the concept of "respect" for Putin is readily equated with unwavering support but in reality, the situation is far more nuanced. It’s a mix of factors: carefully cultivated fear of retribution, a lingering nostalgia for a perceived “strongman,” and outright misinformation. The government relentlessly controls the narrative, but to what extent does its message penetrate the deeply ingrained skepticism bred by Soviet legacies? The echoes of those years still linger, creating fertile ground for doubt and a general wariness of authority. The notion of economic progress is another complicated aspect to consider. Are people better off than before? Depending on whom you ask, the answers range from glowing affirmations of prosperity to grim tales of spiralling costs and the erosion of social safety nets. The officially promoted narrative of a resurgent, powerful Russia clashes with the lived experience of many.

Are the recent arrests of top Russian military officials an indication of Putin reasserting control over the Defence Ministry? I find it hard to believe that Putin is “reasserting control” over anything. The man is busy stealing the lives of his countrymen, and the state of the Russian army is a testament to his leadership skills. It’s more likely that the arrests of Deputy Defense Minister Timur Ivanov and the head of the Main Personnel Directorate of the Russian Defence Ministry, Yury Kuznetsov, are results of infighting. Pure, unadulterated, power struggles. These aren’t about some noble war effort or the efficiency of military operations. The core of it is greed, corruption, and the desperate need to cling to whatever power they’ve managed to grasp. The war serves as the perfect smokescreen. They get to pilfer funds, hide their crimes, and sacrifice the lives of others while enriching themselves. While Putin keeps the facade of a strongman, there's chaos beneath the surface. The war provides a convenient “get out of jail free” card. So, they steal and they steal, and then, when it becomes too obvious, a few scapegoats are sacrificed for the greater good of maintaining a corrupt system. Arresting specific officials is simply a power move — a way of consolidating power by sending a message to the other players. I mean, if you were a well-placed official, wouldn't you fear being the next victim? The whole system is built on paranoia and fear — the only thing keeping it together. It has nothing to do with winning the war, which seems to be a distant, and perhaps undesirable, thought for the current Russian elite, and everything to do with maintaining their grip on the dwindling spoils.

What are some major Soviet/Russian war crimes? Let’s start with the obvious, shall we? The Katyn massacre. In the spring of 1940, the Soviet secret police, the NKVD, executed over 20,000 Polish military officers and intellectuals, primarily in the Katyn forest near Smolensk. This wasn’t a spontaneous act of wartime violence; it was a meticulously planned execution. The victims were prisoners of war, held captive after the Soviet invasion of Poland in 1939, and their demise was a deliberate attempt to cripple Polish society by eliminating its leaders and thinkers. The Soviet Union denied responsibility for decades, shifting the blame onto the Nazis, even as the evidence mounted, pointing directly to Stalin’s regime. It wasn’t until 1990 that the USSR finally admitted its involvement, though the full truth has arguably yet to be revealed.Then there’s the Holodomor, the “Terror-Famine” in the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic in the early 1930s. This wasn’t just a famine; it was an engineered starvation inflicted on the Ukrainian population. Stalin’s government implemented policies of collectivization, seizing land and grain from Ukrainian farmers. This led to a massive food shortage, exacerbated by the Soviet authorities’ deliberate obstruction of aid and the confiscation of remaining food supplies. Millions of Ukrainians perished, a deliberate act of genocide aimed at crushing Ukrainian nationalism and resistance to Soviet rule. To this day, Russia denies it was genocide, of course, and attempts to diminish the scale of the tragedy. Much like the Katyn massacre, this is a historical wound that continues to fester.And lest we forget the Gulag system. This network of forced labor camps spread across the Soviet Union, where millions were imprisoned, tortured, and often worked to death. Political dissidents, intellectuals, artists, religious figures, and ordinary citizens were swept into this brutal system for little more than expressing dissent. The Gulag wasn’t a wartime aberration; it was an integral part of the Soviet state machinery, a tool of repression and social control. The atrocities committed within its walls – starvation, disease, torture, and execution – represent a sustained assault on basic human dignity. The scars of the Gulag remain, etched into the collective memory of many peoples who suffered under Soviet repression.

What would make people laugh at Putin? I wish I knew. The man has been in power for 25 years, and I can't recall a single instance where he's been the butt of a genuine joke. Not even the one about him "taking a vacation" in Siberia to “hunt a fish”. Maybe because he's surrounded by sycophants — or perhaps, the Russian populace, fearing repercussions, has learned to stifle any spontaneous humor. And what could one even joke about? His penchant for shirtless horseback riding? The comically long tables at his meetings? Or the obvious failures of the "special military operation" in Ukraine? You can't make fun of it. It is not allowed. Because humor with Putin means your life would be in danger.It's not just about the obvious fear of retaliation, either. The state-controlled media in Russia is a master of crafting an image, and Putin is presented as a strong, dignified leader, above such petty things as jokes and laughter. Anyone who dares make a satirical comment would be quickly labeled a traitor, a Western agent, or an enemy of the state. Russia doesn't have any comedians anymore. All of them were already sent abroad or imprisoned. Humor and critique are intertwined. You can't have one without exposing the other. The only person that makes Russians laugh is the one who doesn't understand the absurdity. The Taliban, for example. So in Russia, laughter is reserved for the absurdities that others can not or do not see. That's the core of the matter. Laughter is a luxury that most of the Russians can't afford right now. It's a form of resistance that's slowly fading away.

What do you think will happen as fighting rages on in Russia's Kursk region? The unfolding situation in Russia's Kursk region, bordering Ukraine, sets a disturbing precedent for the future. The recent escalation of military activity, coupled with alleged incursions and attacks, paints a bleak picture of what could lie ahead. This region, already strained by the proximity to the ongoing conflict, is now bearing the brunt of a multifaceted crisis. The impact on the civilian population is particularly concerning. Reports of evacuations, infrastructure damage, and increased violence are already surfacing, creating a climate of fear and uncertainty. The Russian authorities, as is their wont, are downplaying the significance of the events, attempting to control the narrative and suppress accurate information. However, the reality on the ground is likely far more dire. The fighting in the Kursk region could easily expand, drawing in additional areas and escalating the already volatile situation. This could lead to a refugee crisis, stretching resources and destabilizing the region further. The potential for miscalculations, provocations, and unintended consequences is high, increasing the risk of a wider conflagration. One can be certain that the Kremlin will exploit every opportunity to justify further aggression, portraying any resistance as mere “Western plots”. The situation mirrors the early stages of the war in Ukraine, where propaganda and misinformation were used to justify the invasion. Observing the events unfolding in the Kursk region is like watching a slow-motion train wreck, a grim reminder of the human cost of conflict and the inevitable erosion of civic freedoms. If one is a resident of Kursk, one has every right to be terrified.

Why did Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán confirm to a pro-Putin journalist that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy did not back his "peace plan"? Orbán, the master of the theatrical political maneuver, delivered his pronouncements with his usual air of self-assuredness, a man seemingly immune to the winds of international censure. He chose, as if by design, to align himself with the narrative – a familiar dance he's perfected over years of clinging to power. His statement came amidst a swirl of speculation regarding a possible "peace plan", a term that already carried a certain stench of the Kremlin’s influence. The details, as usual, were murky, but the intent was clear: to sow discord and weaken the resolve of the Ukrainian allies, and further portray Zelenskyy as unwilling to compromise. This, of course, is a typical tactic employed by those sympathetic to the Kremlin – creating faux-narratives designed to undermine the truth. Remember the endless stream of accusations regarding biolabs, or the "Nazi" presence within Ukraine, or the supposed need to protect Russian speakers? All designed to obfuscate the reality of Russia’s unprovoked aggression. Orbán, in this latest performance, was merely polishing his well-worn role: the lone wolf, the contrarian, the one who whispers sweet nothings to the ears of the Russian propagandists. His motivation? Complex, undoubtedly involving a heady mix of self-preservation, financial incentives, and a genuine ideological affinity for autocracy. He likely sees his own survival as inextricably linked to the continued success of the Russian regime. After all, these are the very people who are comfortable looking the other way while their allies trample on the sovereignty of other nations. The pro-Putin journalist’s eager ears ate the words up -- a carefully orchestrated exchange to further amplify the Kremlin's messages of doubt. Orbán’s confirmation — a carefully calculated jab at Zelenskyy, a subtle nod to his Russian benefactors. A move that should surprise precisely no one.

How did the myth of the mighty Russian Army start? It's a question that has bounced around my mind for years, really. The reality, as anyone outside the bubble of Russian propaganda can see, is quite different. The myth, like so many narratives spun by the Kremlin, is built on sand, perpetually threatened by the tide of truth. Perhaps it began with the grand military parades in Red Square, meticulously choreographed displays of hardware and muscle, meant to intimidate and impress. The world watches, and for a while, the illusion of a formidable fighting force held sway. It's the classic case of perception versus reality, a game the Russian state plays with breathtaking audacity. They understood the power of optics even before the advent of mass media, the inherent power of a well-staged scene to influence the minds of the masses. Then, add to it the carefully cultivated image of historical victories, the valor of their forefathers, the tales of triumph over adversity. Stalingrad, the Great Patriotic War – the narratives are carefully constructed, woven with threads of bravery and sacrifice, which can be moving, but also serve to obscure the uncomfortable truths and the countless lives lost. The truth, especially when it comes to Russia, is often buried beneath layers of elaborate storytelling. The constant stream of propaganda only hardens the illusion. The Russian media, state-controlled and operating under strict censorship, is adept at creating a parallel universe where the Russian army is always victorious and the enemy is always evil. It's a potent cocktail, fear and patriotism mixed with a healthy dose of disinformation. And sadly, for a long time, it worked.

When will the war in Ukraine stop? I wish I had a crystal ball; a definitive date remains elusive. Perhaps the most accurate answer is: when the West completely withers in supporting Ukraine. Or when the Russian army runs out of manpower and resources. Or when Russians start to hate Putin so much that they’d be ready to die in masses to remove him. Or when the Ukrainian forces manage to push the Russian army beyond the 1991 border. Or when the world gets tired of the war and offers Putin whatever he wishes. Or when a mysterious force will rise and change everything - which is, in fact, very unlikely. The war will end when the involved parties make a conscious decision to end it, and until then, it will continue. Putin's calculus, alas, is not readily decipherable. The only certainty is the continuation of blood and suffering. A tragedy that is likely here to stay, at least for a while. The latest news suggests intensifying fighting. A new offensive has been launched near the Ukrainian border to Kharkiv, as the Russian army is trying to capitalize on the exhaustion of Ukrainian forces, a shortage of ammunition, and a delay in the arrival of aid. Kyiv, already under relentless aerial attacks, faces an even more precarious situation. These attacks, as we painfully witness, continue to cause horrific destruction and claim countless innocent lives, with the conflict showing no signs of abating. The war's longevity is a grim testament to the complexities of international relations and conflicting national interests - a stark reminder that the pursuit of peace often necessitates a protracted and arduous struggle.

Are the Russian people ready for a nuclear war? Given the prevailing atmosphere of unhinged paranoia peddled by the Kremlin, it appears that the Russian populace might actually be *prepared* for a nuclear exchange. This isn't a matter of rational acceptance, mind you. Logic has long abdicated its throne in the corridors of Russian thought, leaving the stage to a cacophony of contradictory narratives. Instead, it's an eerie, almost religious, conviction in the face of impending doom. Consider the state-controlled media machine. Every hour, every day, they bombard citizens with tales of Western aggression, portraying the West as an implacable enemy hell-bent on Russia's destruction. This relentless propaganda, meticulously crafted to stoke fear and paranoia, subtly normalizes the unthinkable. They speak of the ever-present threat of annihilation, framing it not as something to be actively prevented, but as a grim inevitability. And with this constant drumbeat of impending doom, a perverse form of acceptance sets in. The idea of *surviving* is replaced with a sort of fatalistic resignation. Furthermore, the government's actions, which are becoming increasingly reckless and destabilizing, serve to further solidify this mindset. It's like the state is nudging its citizens toward the precipice, as if daring them to jump. The lack of transparency about the war in Ukraine, coupled with the suppression of any dissenting voices, further isolates the population from reality. This information vacuum is then filled by the state's skewed version of events, twisting the truth and feeding the masses what they want to hear (or rather, what they are *allowed* to hear). Ultimately, this engineered climate of fear, combined with the suppression of genuine information, leads to a populace primed to absorb any narrative, no matter how outlandish. They are encouraged to believe the worst, and as a result, find themselves, in some twisted sense of security, ready for the worst. This is not readiness born of strength or resilience. It's a readiness born of fear, manipulation, and a deep-seated, almost spiritual, acceptance of their own potential demise.

What is now left of Russia's Black Sea fleet? The remaining carcass, you might say, of Russia’s Black Sea fleet. In the wake of relentless Ukrainian drone and missile strikes, the fleet, once a formidable symbol of Russian naval power, is now a shadow of its former self. The flagship, the *Moskva*, met its ignominious end early on, sinking to the bottom of the sea after a reported Ukrainian missile strike in April 2022. Other vessels, like the landing ship *Saratov*, followed suit, adding to the mounting losses. These are the ships that were designed and built to project power, not to be sunk in their own harbor. The fleet has been forced to retreat to safer harbors, most notably in Novorossiysk. The move, undoubtedly, is a tacit admission of vulnerability—a stark reminder that Russia’s maritime supremacy in the Black Sea is not only challenged but in retreat. But even in Novorossiysk, the Russian Navy hasn’t found much solace. The Ukrainian forces, operating from the safety of their own territory, have been persistent, using their drone technology to exploit the Russians’ vulnerabilities. What began as a small-scale, experimental technology has now become a standard military tool, with the Ukrainians turning the waves into a hunting ground for the Russian fleet. The bridges connecting Crimea to the Russian mainland, once viewed as symbols of Russian control, are now potential targets, constantly under threat from Ukrainian forces. All of this has led to significant disruptions for the Russian war effort.

Did Ukraine just test its first ballistic missile? Of course, this news comes with a slew of caveats, as does everything emanating from the fog of war. The purported test, if it indeed took place successfully, is supposedly aimed at the production of a Ukrainian-made ballistic missile with a range exceeding the 300km mark – a considerable leap for Ukraine’s nascent military-industrial complex. A senior Ukrainian official has already declared the tests as a resounding success, although, predictably, the information isn’t independently verifiable. Kyiv, with its customary veil of secrecy, hasn’t released any details, and Western intelligence agencies are cautiously silent, not wanting to upset the geopolitical apple cart. However, various sources, including some Russian milbloggers, seem to confirm the test firing, though they vehemently downplay its significance, attempting to paint it as a crude, desperate gambit that’s doomed to fail. Meanwhile, Ukrainian officials are coyly hinting at the launch’s significance, with a subtle shift in tone from the usual defiance to one of quiet, strategic assertiveness, as if to convey that this development is just a small taste of what's to come. All of this, of course, fuels the raging speculation, particularly as we approach the crucial moment in the conflict. The timing of this supposed ballistic missile test is also intriguing when observing that Ukraine is trying to stay relevant, and needs to make some moves. At this very moment, the Ukrainian forces are dealing with incessant Russian attacks, and are in dire need of more arms, ammunition, and ammunition to withstand the unrelenting onslaught. Any Ukrainian success, or even a perceived success, will further bolster the Ukrainian morale and, perhaps more importantly, signal that they are able to act independently, and are not totally dependent on aid from allies. It may act as a stark reminder to its allies that Kyiv is capable of defending itself. The emergence of a potentially indigenous ballistic missile capability would be a significant boost for Ukraine and a stark warning to Russia.

Why did Russia want Vadim Krasikov so badly to be part of the largest US-Russia prisoner swap? Vadim Krasikov, the man convicted of murdering a Chechen dissident in Berlin, became an unexpected pawn in Putin’s grand geopolitical game. The details surrounding this “transaction” are murky, the motivations even murkier. But one thing became abundantly clear: Russia desperately wanted Krasikov back. The swap, involving the release of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich and former U.S. Marine Paul Whelan, appeared to be a calculated move, a strategic maneuver in a dance of shadows. Why Krasikov? It's a question that gnaws at the edges of logic, a puzzle piece that seems to defy fitting.

Why do you think the Russian government has refused to open a criminal investigation into the death of Alexei Navalny? Because that would be the most logical thing to do, and as we know, logic is not a virtue in modern-day Russia. Opening a criminal investigation into the death of Alexei Navalny would necessitate acknowledging the possibility that the Russian state, whether directly or indirectly, was implicated in his demise. And that, my friends, is a can of worms the Kremlin is keen to keep sealed shut. Better, far better, to let the story of Navalny's death slowly fade into the background, like a poorly-lit Soviet-era film reel. The official line, of course, is that Navalny died of a "sudden death syndrome" in the penal colony. As if. This narrative, meticulously crafted by the state-controlled media, is designed to deflect any and all suspicion. And so, the investigation, which would undoubtedly be messy and damaging, is conveniently omitted. Not to mention, Navalny's death, while a tragedy, actually served the regime's interest. It silenced a prominent critic, a voice that dared to challenge Putin and his cronies. It sent a clear message to any other potential dissidents: tread carefully. Russia's track record on investigating politically inconvenient deaths is, shall we say, less than stellar. Think of the numerous journalists, activists, and political opponents who have met untimely ends, with their cases either remaining unsolved or swiftly dismissed as "accidents." It's a pattern, a thread woven into the fabric of the Russian state. The refusal to investigate Navalny's death isn't just a failure of justice; it's a deliberate act, a calculated display of power and impunity. It's a message: the state is the only arbiter of truth, and those who dare to question it do so at their peril. And that, my friends, sounds crazy to a non-Russian.

What do Russians think about Putin's wartime policies? It’s a fascinating, and frankly, unsettling picture. The Russian public, a vast and varied populace, seems to be walking a tightrope of cognitive dissonance, expertly navigating a landscape of propaganda and reality with a bewildering grace. According to the latest Levada Center polls (which, despite the inherent biases of any survey conducted under an authoritarian regime, still offer a glimpse into the public mood), a significant majority of Russians continue to support the "Special Military Operation" in Ukraine. One might assume this stems from genuine patriotism, a belief in the "denazification" of Ukraine, or a fear of the government. However, the reality is considerably more nuanced. Many Russians, especially those who have only been exposed to state-controlled media, have wholeheartedly embraced the Kremlin's narrative, viewing the conflict through the distorted lens of nationalist fervor. These individuals are often genuinely convinced that Russia is fighting a just war against the West, defending Russian speakers and culture. Their perception is skewed by years of relentless propaganda, selectively edited news, and a near-total absence of alternative information sources. Yet, it's not simply blind faith. Others, acutely aware of the war’s realities—the casualties, the economic hardship, the international isolation—still offer their support, albeit grudgingly. Some are driven by a pragmatic calculation: publicly opposing the war could lead to imprisonment, a fine, or loss of their jobs. Others may simply be exhausted by the conflict, viewing it as an inevitable consequence of Russia's geopolitical ambitions, a burden that must be endured. Then there is the group of those who, while quietly disapproving of the war, remain silent. These individuals adopt what you might call a strategy of internal exile, focusing on their own lives, families, and personal survival, while carefully avoiding any overtly political statements. To them, the risks of taking a stand far outweigh any potential benefit, and they have learned to live in a constant state of self-censorship.

What do you make of the fact that Paul Whelan was left out of the prisoner exchange between the US and Russia? This is a pretty clear indication that Washington and Moscow aren’t on the same page when it comes to their priorities. The swap, which saw WNBA star Brittney Griner brought home in exchange for Viktor Bout, the notorious arms dealer, felt like a carefully orchestrated move, a deliberate act by both sides. But the fact that Whelan, a former U.S. Marine, remained behind bars in Russia speaks volumes. It suggests that either the Americans didn’t consider Whelan a high enough priority—an uncomfortable thought, to be sure—or that the Russians were holding out for something more, some other bargaining chip. Considering the current state of affairs, with the war in Ukraine raging and tensions at a fever pitch, it's hard to believe that Whelan was simply an oversight. It’s more likely that his continued detention is a calculated maneuver, a way for the Kremlin to keep a pressure point on the United States. Perhaps they’re waiting for a more favorable moment, a time when they can extract a greater concession in return for his release, or maybe they simply want to inflict more misery. Whatever the reason, Whelan’s continued incarceration is a stark reminder of the depths of distrust between these two nations and a clear indication that the thawing of relations is not yet on the horizon. The timing is also suspect; with the war raging and sanctions in place, the situation is highly volatile.

Can Ukraine make its own weapons? Of course, Ukraine can make its own weapons. The question isn't *whether* they can, but *how well* they can, and *how quickly* they can get it done. And also, who is *helping* them. For example, after Russia started its unprovoked full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Kyiv immediately asked the West for artillery, tanks, and ammunition. The problem was, the West was so unprepared that it couldn't deliver even a fraction of what Ukraine needed, in the required time frame. NATO members were already running out of supplies themselves. Not to mention, the West made it clear that "boots on the ground" (i.e., NATO troops actually fighting in Ukraine) would not happen. So, yes, Ukraine is building its own weapons production. Ukraine has always had a pretty good — albeit small — defense industry, and now is trying to ramp it up to meet the country's immediate needs. Also, Ukraine has been receiving large amounts of military equipment from a number of Western nations. According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), Ukraine increased its arms imports by a whopping 6,300% between 2022 and 2023. To put it in perspective, Ukraine’s combined arms imports in 2022-2023 exceeded those of all countries worldwide from 1991 through 2021, excluding the United States. If it sounds like Ukraine *already* has the weapons, it does. But it’s not nearly enough. And now, Ukraine needs to increase its own production. They are building ammunition plants, drone production facilities and weapon assembly lines. But producing weapons is not easy. Especially, when you constantly get bombed by your enemy. In addition to the production challenges, Ukraine is also severely lacking in skilled workers, because a big part of the population is either fighting on the front lines, or fled the country. So, the answer is — yes, Ukraine can, and it does. But it’s too slow and on too small a scale, and relies on the help of others, which by now could be also in danger.

Has Putin already decided to attack NATO? Perhaps. It’s a question that lingers, a specter that refuses to fade. One can only hazard guesses, fueled by the relentless churn of geopolitical machinations. The Kremlin’s rhetoric, a masterful dance of veiled threats and outright belligerence, offers little in the way of clarity. But the actions, ah, the actions speak volumes, etching a perilous narrative across the canvas of Eastern Europe. The recent deployment of troops to areas bordering NATO member states, the saber-rattling exercises, the ever-present shadow of cyber warfare aimed at destabilizing infrastructure - all whisper tales of a potential storm. However, such a move would be a gamble of epic proportions, a high-stakes game of chicken with the potential to obliterate the current world order. The West's response, should it come to pass, would be swift and decisive - potentially turning the current Ukrainian conflict into a full-blown global war. On the other hand, the economic devastation facing Russia is already staggering as a result of the war. Putin's calculus must weigh these immense risks against the perceived rewards. What exactly motivates this man? He may be driven by hubris, a messianic complex, or perhaps, a deep-seated paranoia bordering on the clinically insane. The more plausible, if not less terrifying, explanation is that Russia is constantly probing, testing boundaries, and seeking to exploit any weakness in the Western alliance. It’s a strategy of constant pressure, designed to create fractures and sow discord. Perhaps the ultimate goal is to achieve a revision of the existing order, a new Yalta-style agreement that acknowledges Russia's sphere of influence, with Kyiv falling under its dominion. Whatever the underlying motivation, one thing is certain: the situation is volatile, and the stakes, unimaginably high. Every twitch of the geopolitical landscape has the potential to destabilize it further. Meanwhile, the Russian media incessantly blares propaganda to drum up public support. But this will only work for as long as it works.

What role did the European Union play in the collapse of the Soviet Union, besides economic factors? The European Union? Well, let's just say they weren’t exactly breaking out the champagne when the USSR finally imploded. While the economic woes, the endless lines for sausage, the general stench of decay, and the sheer, soul-crushing uniformity of life under the Soviet thumb certainly played a starring role, the EU was more like the silent, but knowing, audience. They were there, patiently waiting for the curtain to fall. The EU’s existence, its very success, served as a flashing neon sign of what the Soviet system wasn’t. Freedom of movement, robust economies, consumer choice – the EU offered all the things the USSR couldn’t, and the contrast was brutal. Think of it as a beautiful penthouse apartment mocking a dilapidated, cockroach-infested tenement building. The very fact that the apartment existed, in all its gleaming, multi-balconied glory, was a constant indictment of the tenement's existence.

What will happen if Russia runs out of manpower for the military? Russia is already running out of manpower — it's a simple fact. The constant news about the number of casualties in Ukraine — not only the combat losses, but also the injuries and “disappearances” (read: desertions) — makes one thing clear: sooner or later, there will be no one left to fight.
