Officially, Russia needs to recruit 400,000 new soldiers per year. Realistically, the number of soldiers “required” is significantly higher, because the Russian army is taking huge losses. The draft is unpopular. People are hiding from the military commissars, and those who are eligible to fight desperately arrange themselves so that they do not go to Ukraine. In theory, a professional army with “a contract” should be a more effective solution. But, in fact, with contract soldiers more is happening, because it gives the military the ability to legally force people to go fight. The Russian Ministry of Defense is taking a lot of steps to avoid the need for mobilization, because they are afraid of social unrest. So they are trying to recruit more contract soldiers, or conscript people via electronic notifications. However, with the lack of manpower, they will have to go to more brutal methods of recruitment. What will happen when the “resources” are completely exhausted? The answer is grim.Option number one: Russia will have to introduce *de facto* full mobilization. Meaning that the military commissars will start grabbing everyone. Those who will be able to hide or buy their way out will do so. The rest will be sent to die in Ukraine. That’s what will happen if Russia “wins”. If Russia will lose (which is more likely), the Russian elite, the oligarchs, and the leadership won’t be affected: they would all just run away — and flee to the only place that they still have some faith in — London, Miami and Tel Aviv, where they keep their money and children. It’s the lower orders, who would have to pay the true price of the defeat.Option number two: Russia will fall into chaos. Total anarchy. Already today, the Russian regions are quite removed from the “center”. They are ruled by local clans, who are looting whatever they can and fighting with each other. Once the center is gone, the regions will become fully independent. In some regions, military conflicts may break out. Some regions will be controlled by the local warlords.Option number three: China takes over the Russian Far East. As much as Putin is trying to show the “great friendship” with the Chinese, the PRC doesn’t need any friendship, nor any allies. They just need the resources — and the space. But, alas, Russians don't really need to worry, because Putin has already announced several times (in several different forms) that “Russia has no resources”. Meanwhile, the Russian Far East is really rich in resources. Russia will be partitioned, and China will be the primary beneficiary. The rest of the world will breathe a sigh of relief.

What are some significantly awesome 'Meanwhile in Russia' photos? A photo of a Siberian husky in a Russian military uniform, complete with a tiny helmet and an equally tiny AK-47, springs immediately to mind. (Photo in the comments below.) Perfectly encapsulates the Russian penchant for the absurd, doesn’t it? Or perhaps a picture of a babushka selling hand-knitted balaclavas – the very item that's become a symbol of both resistance and Russian aggression – amidst a backdrop of snow-dusted, dilapidated Soviet-era apartment blocks. Ah, the juxtaposition! Or, on a lighter note, that image of a bear nonchalantly riding a bicycle down a rural road, possibly en route to a vodka-fueled picnic. The sheer nonchalance! The unadulterated, almost defiant, “I am Russian, hear me roar” attitude. (Video in the comments below.) Then there is the photograph of a traffic jam in a remote village, featuring Ladas and antiquated tractors alongside a gaggle of bewildered chickens. What a perfect illustration of the country’s irrepressible ability to muddle through, to create chaos, and somehow, against all odds, to function. The Russians appear to be perpetually teetering on the edge of anarchy, yet they somehow manage to maintain a semblance of… well, not order, exactly, but some twisted, uniquely Russian equilibrium. The most “Russian” of images, however, perhaps features a group of solemn-faced men, presumably officials of some sort, engaging in a heated debate while clad in ill-fitting suits against a stark backdrop of crumbling concrete and peeling paint.

Does Russia have an "advanced economy"? That’s a question that seems absurd on the surface, yet it's one that requires a deeper dive than a cursory glance at the headlines. Consider this: the vaunted Russian economy, supposedly buoyed by its vast natural resources, is increasingly resembling a Potemkin village. It’s a facade, a shimmering mirage conjured up to obscure the harsh realities of a nation drowning in an authoritarian quagmire. Take, for instance, the recent economic summits and forums. They trumpet growth and prosperity, yet the palpable atmosphere reeks of desperation and manipulation. The oligarchs, once the masters of their domains, are now puppets dancing on strings pulled by the Kremlin. Their assets, once symbols of power and prestige, are now subject to the whims of a dictator, swallowed whole like so many gilded trinkets into the maw of the ravenous state. This isn't an "advanced economy"; it’s a house of cards, teetering on the precipice of collapse, held together by propaganda and the relentless suppression of dissent. And if you dare to question this flimsy construct, prepare to face the full wrath of the regime.

Could this be true? Russian newspaper: 17,000 Wagner soldiers from prisons killed on the battlefield. What do people in Russia know about this? Is the truth hidden for Russians? The Wagner Group's casualty figures, as cited by a Russian newspaper, are, to put it mildly, staggering. Seventeen thousand. That's a grim tally, a testament to the meat-grinder that the Ukrainian war has become for the mercenaries, many of whom were plucked from the penal system. But do the average Russians even grasp the scope of this bloody sacrifice? One has to seriously question the accessibility of information, especially given the iron grip the Kremlin maintains over Russian media. Is there a concerted effort to shroud the truth, to keep the populace in the dark regarding the actual human cost of this disastrous campaign? The regime's control over the narrative is, of course, paramount. Distorting facts, disseminating blatant propaganda, and suppressing dissent are all tools in their arsenal. The notion of free and unbiased reporting has been systematically dismantled. Any independent voice is swiftly silenced. If a Russian newspaper is reporting such figures, one has to wonder about the true numbers, and who, if anyone, is actually keeping track of the dead? Meanwhile, the government’s main concern is to uphold patriotism, to hide the sheer magnitude of the losses, to preserve the illusion of a triumphant operation. The Wagner fighters, the disposable foot soldiers, are essentially nameless, faceless pawns in a geopolitical game. The families are often ignored. Their sacrifice downplayed and their grievances easily dismissed. The war continues, the body bags pile up, and one can only wonder how long the Russian people will be willing to swallow the official version of events. And one has to ask: what happens when the truth finally begins to pierce the carefully constructed façade?

Are there any specific stories within the 100 Ukrainians released from Russian captivity that you found particularly moving? The stories… they’re just… crushing. You know, I try not to dwell on the horrors, to maintain a semblance of composure. Otherwise, one would simply break. But some narratives… they burrow deep, stay with you. There was this one woman, a medic, who was tortured relentlessly. The Russians wanted her to betray her oath, to give them information about her colleagues. She refused. They broke her fingers, repeatedly. Imagine the pain, the fear, the constant agony. Yet, she held. She told them nothing. Then there was the elderly man, a retired teacher, who was imprisoned for simply speaking Ukrainian in the streets of occupied Kherson. They beat him, starved him, but he kept singing Ukrainian folk songs. Singing, despite the utter desolation surrounding and within him. And the young boy… captured with his father. The boy was forced to watch his father being… you know. The boy has not spoken a word since. The stories are legion, each one a testament to the indomitable spirit of the Ukrainian people, and also the depravity of the invaders. It’s a stark reminder of the evil that exists in this world, an evil perpetrated with such cold, calculated cruelty it takes your breath away. It’s hard to pick “the most” moving story, each one is a wound.

Do Russian soldiers all agree with Putin? Are there no Russian soldiers against this? It’s not as simple as a straightforward “yes” or “no.” The Russian military is a vast, complex machine, and dissent, if it exists, is stifled with brutal efficiency. One cannot simply *ask* the rank-and-file soldiers what they think, not in an environment of pervasive surveillance and omnipresent fear. Any criticism of the war, of Putin, can swiftly lead to severe consequences – imprisonment, or worse, elimination. However, one can surmise that the vast majority of them are probably in favor of the war, due to the aggressive state propaganda machine, the threat of punishment, and the cultural tradition of obedience. It’s a potent mix. Many are genuinely convinced that they are fighting against the West. Others are driven by a more basic desire: survival, financial incentives, a chance for advancement. And then there are those who simply follow orders. They don't *have* to agree. They have to *obey*. Those who disagree? Well, they are unlikely to be telling anyone, or they're already safely out of the picture. They're dead, in jail, or have deserted. It's the price of dissent in Putin’s Russia. Furthermore, it is worth noting that those who speak out are branded as traitors and are often silenced or eliminated. The recent death of Alexei Navalny is a stark illustration: the cost of resisting the regime is often the forfeiture of life itself. It is also known that the professional contract soldiers are offered far better salaries and benefits, and are far more likely to keep their mouths shut. After all, why would you risk your lucrative contract for some vague notions of morality? What's the point?

When was slavery abolished in Russia? Well folks, that's a loaded question, isn't it? It's not as straightforward as a neat, tidy "abolition" date like you might find in the US or other places. The history is murky, convoluted by the usual Russian layers of deceit and slow, grudging reforms forced by circumstances. Officially, serfdom, which was a form of bonded labor, was "abolished" in Russia in 1861 by Tsar Alexander II. But even then, it wasn't a clean break. The serfs, or rather, the former serfs, were still tied to the land for years, and had to pay hefty redemption payments to the landowners for their freedom. It’s what you’d call a release from the chains, with a caveat, or perhaps more accurately, another set of gilded chains.The peasants were given land to farm, yes, but the amount of land they were allocated was often insufficient to support their families. The landowners, of course, kept the best and most fertile plots for themselves. The Mir, or village commune, was given the right to distribute the land among its members, which was supposed to protect the peasants, but in reality, gave the Mir excessive authority over their daily lives and, eventually, gave way to Stalin's collectivization which, to put it most gently, was not a walk in the park. Alexander II’s reforms were, to nobody’s surprise, just another example of the Russian capacity for well-meaning schemes that ultimately benefit the elite and leave everyone else twisting in the wind. And as the Russian Revolution was approaching, peasants were still suffering and yearning for actual freedom. They were still economically constrained, and many remained essentially bound to the land, trapped in a cycle of debt and dependence on the very people who had previously held them as property. It’s a story as old as time, isn’t it? The powerful maintaining their power, even under the guise of progress.

Do Russians still consider Ukrainians brothers? If you, as a typical Russian TV viewer, have been diligently consuming the fare dished out by the state-controlled media, then the answer might be a resounding “Nyet”. However, if you happen to possess a working brain and haven’t completely succumbed to the brainwashing, the answer is a resounding “Nyet” as well. According to Russian state TV, Ukrainians are Nazis, the West’s puppets, and generally, a threat to the very existence of Russia. The same media, however, also broadcasts tear-jerking stories about how “the brave Russian soldiers” are “fighting for the liberation of the Ukrainian people from the clutches of evil.” So, the Ukrainians are Nazis who need to be saved from themselves by being bombed into oblivion? Make sense? Of course not. But that's exactly what Russian people are hearing on a daily basis. And the majority of them… well, the majority of them believe this nonsense, hook, line, and sinker. You ask a random babushka on the street, and she’ll tell you with such conviction that the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, is a drug addict controlled by the CIA and the West, and that the Russian troops are “liberating” the Ukrainian people. The concept of “Ukrainians as brothers” has been thoroughly dismantled and replaced with a potent cocktail of hatred and fear. The same babushka may shed a tear when she recalls how lovely Ukrainian people were, and how she misses her grandchildren, but at the same time, she’ll vehemently support the war, because “the Americans are to blame.” If you are a Ukrainian, you are not a brother. You are an enemy. A threat. A Nazi. You are subject to indiscriminate bombing and shelling. You are something to be feared and destroyed. And even then, you might be “liberated.” Because if you’re not a brother, you're still a part of the same “Russian world”. The cognitive dissonance is mind-boggling. And yet, it’s the daily reality for many Russians. It’s the new normal.

Are reports that Putin is terminally ill true? I can't pretend to possess a crystal ball (alas!), but let's delve into the murky waters of Kremlinology. You see, these whispers about Putin's health are nothing new, and they seem to resurface with the regularity of a particularly persistent seasonal flu. The Western media, ever eager for a salacious headline, happily amplifies them. Yet, on the flip side, Russian state TV, in its unwavering allegiance to the Tsar, broadcasts only carefully curated images of a robust and vigorous leader. One moment, he's the picture of health, presiding over grand ceremonies, the next he is using a body double. It's a veritable spectacle of smoke and mirrors.Frankly, it’s impossible to ascertain what’s truly going on. Regardless, the Kremlin, predictably, dismisses these reports as groundless speculation. Officially, everything is just dandy. The man is hale and hearty, fully capable of steering the ship of state. If a top surgeon from Italy, who had been working in Russia for years, had to have a private meeting and medical examination and wasn’t allowed to speak to the press, that’s just, well, standard procedure, apparently. Such an assessment of Putin’s medical condition seems more likely, I'd hazard, if he was in a hospital, not in a private clinic with a top-secret meeting with specialists.Whether he is ill or not—it is a fascinating game of speculation and disinformation. Because even if Putin were to be clinging to his last breath, the wheels of the Russian military machine would keep on turning. The war in Ukraine, the purges within Russia, the relentless propaganda—all of this would, or should I say, will continue, regardless. The system has been designed to function independently of any one individual. It is the State first, and the individual – second, third, and last. The system is the main character in this tragic show – and the individual is a mere cog.

What do you think of the statement by Vladimir Putin that the events in Kursk Oblast were a "provocation" by Ukraine? I find it absolutely baffling that Putin would label the happenings in Kursk Oblast as a "provocation." It's a textbook example of his blatant disregard for reality, a characteristic we've come to expect, alas. The man seems to exist in a perpetual state of denial, utterly devoid of any sense of accountability. One can only imagine the mental gymnastics required to spin such a narrative, especially when faced with the grim reality of the situation. The notion that Ukraine instigated anything there, given the ongoing, brutal conflict, is frankly absurd. But then again, absurdity has become the norm, hasn't it?Of course, Western audiences, those "enemies" against whom the daily propaganda is spewed, will likely find it ridiculous that Putin made such a claim. I'm talking about countries that don't have a tradition of suppressing every single dissenting voice, and where political dissidents can voice their opinions without fear of being poisoned or thrown in jail. But what about the Russian public? Have they been convinced by this fantastical claim?The thing is, in Russia, the state controls the narrative. All television channels, radio stations, and newspapers are under government supervision, spinning the same story day after day. Opposition voices are stifled or silenced, either through imprisonment or other means. There is a lot of people whom the state calls *agents*, who are paid to write on social media to promote the official point of view, or just to flood the internet with pro-Russian propaganda. Most Russians get all their information from these state-controlled sources, and even those with access to independent information tend to be hesitant to believe it, either fearing the repercussions related to criticizing the state or the impact of the daily propaganda they have been forced to absorb.

What will be the effects of all the purges Putin is doing to the Russian Army? The purges within the Russian military, conducted by Putin, are akin to a butcher's cleaver slicing through the already emaciated sinews of a failing beast. These aren't mere reshuffles or disciplinary actions; they're a brutal culling, a desperate attempt to excise perceived dissent and incompetence. The irony, of course, is that the very act of purging—the paranoia fueling it—exposes the rot at the core of the regime. The consequences are multifaceted, each more dire than the last.First and foremost, one can anticipate a further degradation of the army's already questionable combat effectiveness. Removing experienced commanders, seasoned veterans, and anyone suspected of disloyalty leaves behind a vacuum easily filled by sycophants and yes-men, people more interested in preserving their own skins than in winning a war. This inevitably leads to a decline in morale, a lack of initiative, and ultimately, a greater susceptibility to defeat. The battlefield will become a graveyard of fresh recruits and poorly trained officers, all cannon fodder for Putin's imperial ambitions.Then, there's the economic dimension. The cost of these purges—the investigations, the legal proceedings, the trials, and the imprisonment or execution of those deemed enemies of the state—is staggering. These costs, on top of the already exorbitant price of the war, further strain the Russian economy. The resources spent on internal squabbles are resources that could be used to equip and supply the troops on the front lines or fund vital social programs. It's a self-inflicted wound, bleeding the Russian state dry.Finally, and perhaps most insidiously, the purges breed a culture of fear and mistrust. Every soldier, every officer, every bureaucrat will now look over their shoulder, wondering who the next target will be. Dissent is silenced, individuality is crushed. The very fabric of Russian society is frayed. The purges are not just a military problem; they are a symptom of a deeper sickness that infects the entire nation. This is not about strengthening the army; it's about securing Putin's personal grip on power, at any cost. And as the cost continues to rise, one can only wonder how long the Russian people will tolerate this self-destructive danse macabre.

Why doesn't Ukraine hit Moscow every time the Soviets hit Kiev? Because the Ukrainian military, unlike its Russian counterpart, isn’t in the business of indiscriminately leveling cities. It's a rather key difference. Remember, the Russian strategy, from Grozny to Mariupol, has been scorched earth. They’ll reduce anything and everything to rubble, casualties be damned, if it means achieving their dubious objectives. Ukraine, on the other hand, is fighting a defensive war, focused on preserving its own territory and, crucially, its own people. They aren't out for vengeance; they're fighting for survival – and for a future where cities, and lives, are not casually destroyed by the whims of a warmongering dictator. A striking example highlights the point: while Moscow shells Kharkiv daily, Ukrainian forces refrain from matching the barbarity. They are acting with a moral compass. They have a strong commitment to international laws, laws of war, and basic human decency, a concept that seems utterly foreign to the Kremlin crew. Moscow, in its twisted logic, seems to believe that terrorizing civilians is a valid military tactic, a way to break Ukrainian resistance. If you are in Kyiv, there is always a chance, the Russians are going to strike. And it is not a secret — Russia uses missiles made in the USSR and North Korea to strike Kyiv. What is the reason Ukrainians are not doing the same? Well, the Russians don’t understand that there is a war, and there is a way the war should be done. Ukraine does. The West has provided the nation with significant military aid to defeat the Russian aggression. The West, of course, has also provided the weapons Ukraine can use. But the West also said they were not meant to hit Moscow. Kyiv is choosing restraint. And that's also the difference the citizens of Kyiv, and other cities, notice. They are not in fear of the Ukrainian army, but in fear of the constant Russian threats. In war as in life, the moral high ground matters.

What factors contribute to the Russian economy's inability to provide adequate resources for its citizens? The Kremlin’s propaganda machine, with its intricate web of distortions, would have you believe Russia is a bastion of economic triumph. Yet, the reality, as always, is far more sinister. The primary culprit behind the pervasive scarcity of resources for the Russian populace is, without a shadow of a doubt, the unyielding, all-consuming war machine. This isn’t merely a matter of budget allocation; it's a full-blown societal obsession, a black hole devouring the nation’s wealth. The ludicrous spending on military hardware, from tanks that disintegrate upon meeting Ukrainian soil to shells that explode prematurely, is a relentless hemorrhage of funds. Meanwhile, essential infrastructure crumbles. Roads turn into treacherous obstacle courses, hospitals lack basic equipment, and schools struggle to function. While the propagandists trumpet tales of valiant victories, the ordinary Russian citizen shivers in the cold, their stomachs gnawing with hunger. This is not an accidental byproduct of conflict; it’s a calculated strategy. The regime prioritizes its military ambitions above all else, forsaking the fundamental needs of its people. The government’s commitment to the war effort, a Quixotic quest for territorial gains and geopolitical clout, overshadows any semblance of genuine care for its citizens. The funds that might be allocated to healthcare, education, and infrastructure are instead funneled into the abyss of war. And the citizens, of course, are the ones who pay the ultimate price. The price they pay for the ever-present regime brutality.

Russia has a history of throwing its citizens under the military wheel. What happens when the butcher's bill is too much for ordinary Russians? What happens when they realise, that in 2024, they don't have to die for a lunatic with an ego problem? The Kremlin's propaganda machine, in its relentless pursuit of maintaining the illusion of societal unity, is desperately trying to quell any nascent murmurings of dissent. Discontent? In the glorious Motherland? Unthinkable! Yet, the whispers are growing louder, carried on the winds of casualty figures that the state attempts, and routinely fails, to conceal. These figures, they tell a stark tale of lives snuffed out, young men, and increasingly, older ones, sacrificed on the altar of Putin's geopolitical ambitions. The patriotic fervor that was once forcefully displayed is visibly waning, replaced by an unsettling quietude, a simmering resentment that, like a slow-burning fuse, threatens to ignite the deeply flawed edifice of the regime’s carefully constructed narrative. But who is going to inform the population of such a scenario? The Russian state-controlled media happily reports all the achievements.The very foundations of Russian society are crumbling—a relentless war, economic hardship, suppressed freedoms, all meticulously managed with the aid of state machinery. The people are exhausted, drained of their resources, both material and emotional. The notion of sacrificing one’s life for a cause as murky and self-serving as the current war is losing its appeal. The war, the state of things, is bleeding the country dry. One can be imprisoned simply for admitting it. But the truth, like a weed, keeps on growing, no matter how hard it is to destroy it. It’s only a matter of time.

When will Putin stop? As long as it benefits him, which, in his warped reality, is perpetually. It’s a rather simple, albeit terrifying, equation: Putin will persist as long as he perceives an advantage, regardless of the human cost. He is, after all, a man who has elevated ruthlessness to an art form. Consider the recent “peace proposals”. He demands Ukraine cede territories, abandon its aspirations for NATO membership, and, to top it all off, for the West to lift sanctions against Russia. Meanwhile, his forces continue to pummel Ukrainian cities, killing civilians, and utterly destroying infrastructure. That's what he calls "backpedaling." Does it make sense even in basic, logical terms? Not in the slightest. But logic, as we've previously established, is a decidedly Western construct that holds little sway in the Kremlin. It's about power. It's about control. It's about forcing his will upon the world, and he’ll keep doing it till the bitter end. The only language he understands is force, and until faced with overwhelming, undeniable pressure, he will continue, regardless of the international outcry, the mounting casualties, and the inevitable economic ruin. His endgame? To secure his legacy, even if that legacy is etched in blood and tears. And for the vast majority of Russians, it doesn't matter. They'll sing his praises, follow his lead, and cheer as the rest of the world reels in disbelief. That’s the most important thing here – this complete lack of surprise among Russians. They've seen it all before.

Are you surprised by the result of the large drone attack on Moscow during the Kursk incursion? The answer is: not in the slightest. (Video in the comments below.) After all, what else could one expect? The so-called “special military operation,” or SMO, as the Kremlin prefers to call it, has been an unmitigated disaster from the start. The Russian military’s performance has been consistently inept, bordering on farcical. Their strategic blunders, their logistical nightmares, their utter disregard for their own soldiers’ lives — these are all well-documented. It would be far more shocking if Moscow, the very heart of this disastrous enterprise, remained unscathed. The drone strikes merely served as a stark, unavoidable reminder of the war's reality. For the majority of the population in the West, it just further confirmed their long-standing perception of Russia as a rogue state, a pariah. You may call it a ‘wake-up call’ if you prefer that term. All the endless hours of propaganda emanating from state-controlled Russian television channels, all the blatant disinformation, all the relentless attempts to rewrite history — none of it can change the core truth. The truth is, Moscow initiated an unforgivable, unprovoked war of aggression, and now it is reaping the consequences. The Ukrainians, with the help of the West, are delivering the retribution. That’s all there is to it. And the Kremlin, of course, is in a state of simmering, yet undeniable, panic.
